$comment: Canada, Criminal Law - THE FIRST POPULATED AUTHORITY GRAPH ENTRY FOR CANADA. Section 34's unified self-defence test (2013 reform) and its first Supreme Court construction, holding that the 'role in the incident' factor requires holistic assessment of the accused's conduct across the whole incident, not just the moment force was used. CanLII and the SCC's own decisions mirror both returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch this session; the case's holding was corroborated via independent secondary sources and further confirmed via WebSearch by this session.

authorities.name: Criminal Code, s.34
authorities.citation: Criminal Code, RSC 1985, c C-46, s.34(1), (2)(c)
authorities.court: N/A - primary legislation (federal, uniform across Canada)
authorities.date_note: Date of the substantial 2013 reform that replaced the prior multi-provision self-defence scheme with the current unified s.34. The text verified this session is the current in-force version (current to 2026-06-21 per the source page).
authorities.proposition: A person is not guilty of an offence if they believe on reasonable grounds that force or a threat of force is being used against them or another, the act is committed for the purpose of defending against that force, and the act is reasonable in the circumstances (s.34(1)). Reasonableness under s.34(1)(c) is assessed against a non-exhaustive list of factors including the person's role in the incident (s.34(2)(c)), among others such as the nature of the threat, imminence, and proportionality of the response.
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live and directly this session, on two independent passes, word-for-word consistent both times.

authorities.name: R. v. Khill
authorities.judge_or_panel: Martin J. (majority, joined by Wagner CJ, Abella, Karakatsanis, Kasirer JJ); Moldaver J. (concurring, joined by Brown, Rowe JJ); Côté J. (dissenting)
authorities.proposition: The Supreme Court's first construction of the reformed s.34, holding that 'role in the incident' under s.34(2)(c) is not limited to unlawful conduct or provocation - it requires the jury to weigh the accused's conduct across the entire incident, from beginning to end, including conduct that was not independently unlawful but increased the risk of a violent confrontation. On the facts, the trial judge's failure to instruct the jury to consider the accused's decisions not to call police, to retrieve and load a firearm, and to confront a suspected intruder rather than retreat was a reversible error of law, since the jury might have reached a different verdict on reasonableness had it considered his conduct from the start of the incident. Appeal dismissed, new trial ordered.
